tooth-enamel.prompt: Can a missing piece of enamel grow back?

options.a: No, but early weakened areas can become stronger.
options.b: Yes, if you brush harder.
options.c: Yes, saliva can fill the gap.
options.d: Yes, if the tooth does not hurt.

tooth-enamel.explanation: Enamel is the hard outer covering of a tooth. Early damage can sometimes improve, but a missing piece cannot grow back.

tooth-pulp.prompt: What is inside the soft center of a tooth?

options.a: Only hard enamel.
options.b: Nerves and blood vessels.
options.c: Bits of food.
options.d: A layer of plaque.

tooth-pulp.explanation: The soft center is called the pulp. The layers around it help protect these nerves and blood vessels.

plaque-acids.prompt: How can plaque cause a cavity?

options.a: It wears teeth down when you chew.
options.b: It stops teeth from growing.
options.c: Its bacteria use sugar and make acids that weaken teeth.
options.d: It dries out the tooth.

plaque-acids.explanation: Plaque is a sticky layer of bacteria. Some bacteria use sugar and make acids; repeated acid attacks can eventually cause a hole.

early-minerals.prompt: A dentist finds early damage before a hole has formed. What may help?

options.a: Waiting until it hurts.
options.b: Brushing only when the tooth feels rough.
options.c: Avoiding all cold food.
options.d: Fluoride toothpaste, daily cleaning, and less sugar.

early-minerals.explanation: These habits can help an early weakened area become stronger or stop getting worse. Keep the follow-up visits your dentist recommends.

plaque-between-meals.prompt: You have not eaten for a few hours. What happens to plaque?

options.a: It can stay on your teeth, so regular cleaning still matters.
options.b: It disappears on its own.
options.c: It turns into healthy enamel.
options.d: It can no longer affect your teeth or gums.

plaque-between-meals.explanation: Plaque does not disappear between meals. Brushing and cleaning between teeth help remove it.

plaque-low-sugar.prompt: You eat fewer sweets. Why do you still need to brush?

options.a: Brushing is only needed after dessert.
options.b: Plaque can still build up and harm teeth and gums.
options.c: Brushing is only for fresh breath.
options.d: Teeth only need cleaning if they hurt.

plaque-low-sugar.explanation: Eating less sugar helps protect teeth, but it does not remove plaque. Keep brushing with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between teeth.

sipping-frequency.prompt: Why is sipping a sugary drink all afternoon hard on teeth?

options.a: Only the total sugar amount matters.
options.b: Each sip gives bacteria more sugar to make acid.
options.c: Small sips protect teeth from sugar.
options.d: Only the temperature of the drink matters.

sipping-frequency.explanation: Repeated sips mean repeated contact with sugar. Having a sweet drink with a meal avoids prolonged sipping, but the total amount of sugar still matters.

sugar-free-acid.prompt: Can a sugar-free drink still harm teeth if it is acidic?

options.a: Yes, the drink's acids can wear away the tooth surface.
options.b: No, sugar-free always means safe for teeth.
options.c: Only if the drink is warm.
options.d: No, acids make enamel stronger.

sugar-free-acid.explanation: Sugar-free does not mean acid-free. Acids in a drink can damage teeth directly, even without sugar.

dual-exposure.prompt: A drink contains sugar and acids. Why can both be a problem?

options.a: Only the sugar can affect teeth.
options.b: Only the acids already in the drink can affect teeth.
options.c: Bacteria use the sugar to make acid, and the drink already contains acid.
options.d: The sugar makes the acids harmless.

dual-exposure.explanation: Bacteria can turn sugar into acids that weaken teeth. The drink's own acids can also wear away the surface.

saliva-role.prompt: How does saliva help protect your teeth?

options.a: It removes stuck-on plaque.
options.b: It rebuilds chipped enamel.
options.c: It replaces the fluoride in toothpaste.
options.d: It makes acids less harmful and supplies minerals.

saliva-role.explanation: Saliva helps wash away loose food and makes the mouth less acidic. Its minerals can help strengthen early weakened areas, but it cannot replace brushing.

options.a: It removes plaque without brushing.
options.b: It replaces cleaning between teeth.
options.c: It helps strengthen enamel and protect against decay.
options.d: It fills a hole in a tooth.

fluoride-role.explanation: Fluoride helps protect the hard outer surface of teeth. It supports repair of early damage, but cannot fill a hole.

dry-mouth.prompt: Your mouth stays dry after starting a medicine. What should you do?

options.a: Stop the medicine yourself.
options.b: Ask a dentist or doctor for advice.
options.c: Stop brushing until it improves.
options.d: Ignore it unless a tooth hurts.

dry-mouth.explanation: Saliva helps protect teeth, so ongoing dry mouth is worth discussing. Do not stop a prescribed medicine without medical advice.

early-detection.prompt: A new mark on your tooth does not hurt. What should you do?

options.a: Arrange a dental check rather than wait for pain.
options.b: Wait until it becomes painful.
options.c: Scrape it with a sharp tool.
options.d: Assume the tooth is healthy.

early-detection.explanation: Tooth decay can be painless at first. A dentist can check the change and explain whether care is needed.

lost-structure.prompt: Can fluoride toothpaste fill an existing hole in a tooth?

options.a: Yes, after a few days.
options.b: Yes, if you use a large amount.
options.c: No, keep using it and get advice from a dentist.
options.d: Only if the hole is dark.

lost-structure.explanation: Fluoride still helps protect teeth, but missing tooth material will not grow back. A dentist can advise how to care for the hole.

dark-spot.prompt: You notice a dark spot on a tooth. What does it mean?

options.a: It is always a cavity.
options.b: It is harmless if there is no pain.
options.c: It always needs a filling.
options.d: Color alone cannot tell you; a dentist needs to check.

dark-spot.explanation: A dark spot may be a stain or a sign of decay. Its color alone does not show what is happening inside the tooth.

lesion-arrest.prompt: Your dentist says an area of decay has stopped getting worse. Must the mark disappear?

options.a: Yes, otherwise the care has failed.
options.b: No, a mark can remain even when the damage has stopped.
options.c: Yes, it must turn white.
options.d: No, because every dark mark is harmless.

lesion-arrest.explanation: A mark can remain after decay stops getting worse. Keep up daily care and the checks your dentist recommends.

stable-lesion.prompt: A weakened area has not worsened at recent dental checks. What should you do next?

options.a: Stop using fluoride toothpaste.
options.b: Cancel all future checks.
options.c: Judge the tooth only by its color.
options.d: Keep up daily care and agreed dental checks.

stable-lesion.explanation: No recent change is encouraging, but it does not guarantee the tooth will stay the same. Daily care and follow-up still matter.

brushing-routine.prompt: What is a helpful everyday brushing routine?

options.a: Brush once a day with plenty of pressure.
options.b: Clean only the front surfaces.
options.c: Use mouthwash instead of brushing.
options.d: Brush gently twice daily with fluoride toothpaste; spit out the excess.

brushing-routine.explanation: Brush for about two minutes, including before bed, and cover every surface. Spit out excess paste without immediately rinsing with water, so fluoride stays on teeth longer.

between-teeth.prompt: A brush for cleaning between teeth feels too tight. What should you do?

options.a: Push it through harder.
options.b: Try a comfortably fitting tool or floss, and ask for advice.
options.c: Stop cleaning between teeth altogether.
options.d: Use a sharp object instead.

between-teeth.explanation: Do not force a brush between teeth. A dental professional can help you choose a suitable size or show you how to use floss.

tailored-care.prompt: How often should you have a dental check?

options.a: Agree a schedule with your dentist for your needs.
options.b: Only when a tooth hurts.
options.c: Use your friend's schedule.
options.d: Never, if you brush twice a day.

tailored-care.explanation: People have different dental needs. Your dentist can suggest a schedule based on your teeth, gums, and risk of problems.
